items.title: U.S. ready to slap tariffs on China, EU and others over subsidized production, AP sources say
items.description: The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and 14 other economies, according to sources.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[President Donald Trump speaks during an event to announce new tariffs in the Rose Garden at the White House, April 2, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Mark Schiefelbein</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and 14 other economies, according to sources.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — The Trump administration is expected to soon announce plans to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and 14 other economies, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The U.S. Trade Representative’s Office is expected to release the results of a monthslong tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies by the 16 economies in the coming days, according to the people who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

They stressed the timing for the rollout of the tariffs could still change. The White House and USTR did not respond to requests for comment.

Plans for the new tariffs are part of an effort to replace broader duties the administration set last year that were subsequently struck down by the Supreme Court. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.

The tariffs are in response to what the White House has said is excessive manufacturing output in those countries, boosted by subsidies, that has led to a flood of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies.

The anticipated action constitutes a second step in the administration’s efforts to replace the duties announced in April 2025 that the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional in February. The White House slapped 60 trading partners with levies of 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent in July, charging that they have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.

The anticipated trade action demonstrates that the Trump administration is still willing to impose import taxes despite a sweeping loss for the Republican Party in this month’s midterm elections, fueled largely by affordability concerns as inflation remains elevated. At the same time, the new duties could test how the Democrats will respond to tariffs imposed unilaterally by Trump.

Even with majorities in both the House and Senate, Trump could veto any legislation that overturns or waters down the tariffs.

The excess industrial capacity probes were initiated under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the president to levy tariffs against nations that discriminate against U.S. companies or commerce.

The levels of the anticipated tariffs were not immediately clear, but would come on top of tariffs of 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent announced earlier this year.

Many countries, including China, had protested those tariffs, which took effect just as the clock ran out on temporary levies Trump had turned to after the Supreme Court in February struck down sweeping “reciprocal” tariffs he levied on nearly every U.S. trade partner.

The expected move comes as Trump just last week visited the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen for his third face-to-face engagement with Chinese President Xi Jinping this year. Xi’s expected to travel to Doral, Florida, next month for the Group of 20 Summit, which Trump is hosting.

While Trump has moved to build a closer relationship with Xi, the yawning trade deficit remains a significant irritant in the U.S.-China relationship.

Massive capacity in a slew of Chinese industries, from autos to solar panels, cement and steel manufacturing, has drawn increased attention from Beijing’s trading partners in recent years.

Although China’s own leaders have prioritized rebalancing the economy, slowing domestic demand has prompted companies to expand into overseas markets. Surging exports pushed China’s trade surplus to a record of nearly US$1.2 trillion last year.

Chris Rugaber, Aamer Madhani and Josh Boak, The Associated Press

items.title: Chinese tech giant Huawei is guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, U.S. jury finds
items.description: A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.

(AP Photo/Larry Neumeister)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Larry Neumeister</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.
items.body:
NEW YORK — A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world’s biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks.

But jurors acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy, a result that the company’s lawyer said was a “profound rejection” of the government’s narrative that it was corrupt from top to bottom and had a corporate culture of cheating, stealing and lying.

Prosecutors had used the charge, commonly found in organized crime and drug cases, to accuse Huawei of operating illicitly to poach intellectual property and technological secrets from competitors and partners.

The convictions covered allegations that the company did business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions — including Iran and North Korea — and made false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds.

Huawei faces potentially billions of dollars in penalties

In all, Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 counts. The case involved no human defendants, but the company could be made to pay billions of dollars in penalties when it is sentenced next September.

“Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering U.S. national security, violating the sanctity of U.S. commerce, and impeding the enforcement of U.S. laws,” Brooklyn U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said in a statement.

“No person or company is above the law,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said.

Huawei’s lawyers said U.S. investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of the company’s more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that didn’t actually exist.

Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig said the company would appeal the convictions but was heartened by the acquittals on racketeering conspiracy and another charge, conspiracy to obstruct justice. He called those not guilty verdicts “a profound rejection of the United States’ narratives of what Huawei is” and “a vindication of the company and its good-faith compliance culture.”

“The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hardworking company that we came to know and deeply respect,” Heberlig said outside federal court in Brooklyn.

U.S. restrictions haven’t stopped Huawei’s worldwide growth

It’s unclear what effect the verdict might have on Huawei’s global fortunes. The company hasn’t been allowed to sell equipment to U.S. carriers for years because of security concerns. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.

That hasn’t stopped the company from doing a robust business elsewhere. Its smartphones and other telecom equipment are sold globally. More recently, it has expanded into chipmaking as the boom in artificial intelligence fuels demand for microprocessors, becoming an important alternative in China to chips made by companies such as Nvidia.

“Huawei has always adhered to integrity in business, upheld business ethics, respected intellectual property, and remained committed to complying with all applicable laws and regulations,” the company said in a statement.

“We remain focused on serving our customers and partners and ensuring continuous and stable business operations,” the statement said.

The U.S. announced its criminal charges against Huawei in early 2019 and later expanded the allegations. The lengthy trial began in September.

Chinese officials said the U.S. has engaged in “economic bullying” and improperly used national security as a pretext for oppressing Chinese companies.

The U.S. alleged a pattern of theft reaching all the way to the top

The indictment against Huawei accused it of a long pattern of outright technology thefts.

Huawei, prosecutors said, once sold internet routers containing source code copied from a competitor. In another episode, a person working for Huawei slipped into a competitor’s booth at a Chicago trade show to surreptitiously photograph the circuits inside another company’s networking device, the indictment said.

Prosecutors said that on another occasion, a Huawei worker removed a robotic arm from a competitor’s lab so it could be photographed and measured.

The victim companies included Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu, according to court records.

“The tone was set at the top by Huawei leaders and executives who themselves engaged in criminal conduct, like lying to Congress, lying to banks, violating U.S. sanctions and trying to interfere with the very criminal investigation that led to this case,” prosecutor Meredith Arfa told the jury at the trial.

In its statement, Huawei referred to those matters as “trade secret-related disputes” that were the subject of civil litigation that was resolved over the past two decades.

“No court ever found Huawei liable for willful intellectual property misappropriation, and the company was never ordered to pay damages for trade secret misappropriation,” the company said.

Huawei says it isn’t defined by isolated allegations of wrongdoing

In his closing argument to jurors, Huawei’s lawyer said prosecutors leaned on “innuendo and facts ripped out of context,” and testimony from ex-employees “with a bone to pick,” to pursue a company that had relied on “hard work, innovation and competition” to succeed.

“Huawei didn’t steal its way to success,” Heberlig said, noting that much of the material the U.S. alleges was stolen was already public.

“You can’t steal a secret that isn’t a secret,” he said.

He said Huawei paid billions of dollars in licensing fees over the years, with 75 per cent of that money going to U.S. companies, and had reprimanded or fired employees found to have engaged in wrongdoing.

Heberlig noted that lines of Cisco source code turned up in Huawei software more than two decades ago. He said when the source-code copying was discovered, Huawei recalled routers sold in the U.S. and offered to replace them with Cisco routers and created a “compliance culture that permeates Huawei today.”

Charges against Huawei’s finance chief ended in a deal

No individual executives or employees faced trial, although prosecutors at one point also brought criminal charges against Huawei’s chief financial officer, Meng Wanzhou. They accused her of misleading HSBC bank about the company’s business dealings in Iran.

Meng, the daughter of Huawei’s founder, was arrested in Canada in 2018, but ultimately was allowed to return to China in 2021 in a prisoner swap that freed two Canadians held by China. As part of the deal, the U.S. dropped its case against Meng.

The trial in New York overlapped with a summit meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin in the technology-centric city of Shenzhen, China.

Michael R. Sisak And Larry Neumeister, The Associated Press

Associated Press writer Jennifer Peltz contributed.

items.title: Canada and Qatar sign agreement to boost investment
items.description: Canada and Qatar have signed a new agreement that looks to encourage increased investment, despite widespread criticism of Qatar’s human rights record.

THE CANADIAN PRESS/Sean Kilpatrick]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Sean Kilpatrick</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Canada and Qatar have signed a new agreement that looks to encourage increased investment, despite widespread criticism of Qatar’s human rights record.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Canada and Qatar have signed a new agreement that looks to encourage increased investment, despite widespread criticism of Qatar’s human rights record.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and her Qatari counterpart Dr. Ahmad bin Mohammed Al-Sayed signed the Canada-Qatar Foreign Investment Promotion and Protection Agreement in Ottawa on Tuesday.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu, who led negotiations on the agreement, said he’s proud to see the deal signed because it means more Qatari investment in Canada and more opportunities for Canadian businesses in Qatar.

Sidhu said in a media statement that Qatar’s economy is worth nearly $300 billion. He said the Qatar Investment Authority is one of the world’s largest sovereign wealth funds, with nearly US$600 billion in assets.

Canada and Qatar’s bilateral trade exceeds $350 million, said Sidhu, who added that foreign direct investment from Qatar has reached $338 million.

“With this agreement, we’re going to grow that figure,” he said. “The opportunity here is real.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney visited Doha in January, becoming the first sitting Canadian prime minister to visit Qatar. He made the trip after visiting Beijing.

Conservative MP Shuv Majumdar chided Carney on the platform X over his outreach to both China and Qatar, citing their dire human rights records and past support for Canada’s adversaries.

“They traffic in the worst elements of the world because they turn these assets they’ve built up into the indispensable dependencies,” Majumdar said. He said Canada should instead boost trade ties with Taiwan and Arab countries that have normalized relations with Israel.

Human Rights Watch still raises numerous concerns about Qatar, citing slave labour resulting in migrant work deaths, restrictions on free expression and increasing surveillance.

The country chafed at widespread criticism of its treatment of migrant workers and its human rights record in the lead-up to its 2022 hosting of the FIFA World Cup. During that event, Qatar’s officials barred the entry of articles of clothing with rainbows — including items without LGBTQ+ themes.

Sidhu was in Qatar just ahead of Carney’s visit. Sidhu said while he was in Doha, he pitched Canadian projects to the Qatar Investment Authority and the two countries agreed to launch a Canada-Qatar business council.

“The Gulf is one of the most important regions in the world as we work to attract $1 trillion in new investment to Canada and double our non-U.S. exports over the next decade,” said Sidhu. “That investment will build major projects here at home. And it will create good-paying jobs for Canadian workers.”

“We’re moving fast to diversify our trade relationships and build a stronger, more resilient Canadian economy, and this agreement is another step forward.”

Qatar has said it serves as a mediator in international talks with the Taliban. The Taliban have maintained a political office in Qatar for years, including during the period immediately prior to their takeover of Afghanistan in 2021.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

-With files from Dylan Robertson, Kyle Duggan and The Associated Press

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

items.title: Stellantis suing Unifor, accuses union of blocking access to Brampton plant
items.description: Automaker Stellantis is taking legal action against Unifor, claiming the union is blocking the company’s access to its idled Brampton, Ont. plant, which it needs to conduct an environmental assessment as part of its sale to defence company Roshel.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Unifor members rally outside the idled Stellantis assembly plant in Brampton, Ont., on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Arlyn McAdorey]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Arlyn McAdorey</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Automaker Stellantis is taking legal action against Unifor, claiming the union is blocking the company’s access to its idled Brampton, Ont. plant, which it needs to conduct an environmental assessment as part of its sale to defence company Roshel.
items.body:
OTTAWA - Automaker Stellantis is taking legal action against Unifor, claiming the union is blocking the company’s access to its idled Brampton, Ont. plant, which it needs to conduct an environmental assessment as part of its sale to defence company Roshel.

The Toronto Star was first to report the development, and CTV News has since obtained the statement of claim.

According to the statement of claim, filed on Nov. 19, the company is seeking an injunction to stop alleged obstruction to the property. Stellantis is alleging that representatives from Unifor “have sought to prevent the environmental work from proceeding by blocking entrances to the premises” and refusing to allow the environmental consulting firm Pinchin Ltd. from accessing the site.

The statement of claim points to one incident on Nov. 9, in which representatives of Unifor allegedly “blocked entrances with trucks, pylons and individuals carrying Unifor flags” and refused to leave despite the automaker contacting police.

“To date, Unifor has continued to obstruct access by persons associated with the environmental work, and Pinchin has not been permitted to perform the environmental work,” the claim states.

In a statement to CTV News on Tuesday, Stellantis says it is taking “appropriate steps” to access the property.

“Unifor is currently blocking access to the Stellantis Brampton Assembly Plant, preventing scheduled environmental assessment work at the site,” spokesperson LouAnn Gosselin wrote.

Unifor National President Lana Payne, meanwhile, told CTV News she is continuing to “try and get a different outcome,” adding the sale of the plant is “unacceptable” to the union.

“Unifor has been demonstrating in support of Canadian jobs at the Brampton plant throughout the past year,” Payne wrote in an email.

Stellantis’ sale gains attention

Stellantis’ car assembly plant in Brampton has garnered lots of attention in recent weeks, after the automaker announced it was selling the plant to Roshel, a Canadian armoured vehicle manufacturer. The plant has been idle since 2023, with more than 2,200 workers on lay-off pay.

Following the announcement, CTV News reported officials within Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government were actively part of discussions leading up to the agreement to sell, despite Carney calling the sale a “betrayal” and later a “partial solution.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, for her part, has both threatened to sue Stellantis for hundreds of millions of dollars, while also saying the company could be eligible for more taxpayer funds to support workers, if it agrees not to sell the plant.

Last Friday, Stellantis’ global CEO Antonio Filosa met with Joly, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Unifor in a closed-door meeting that Ford described as “challenging but productive.”

The premier also said that Stellantis conveyed during the meeting that, in addition to the U.S. tariffs, a number of policies were making Canada less competitive. The policies include the cost of greenhouse gas emissions and the zero-emission vehicle mandates in B.C. and Quebec.

After that meeting, all parties agreed to continue further talks. A senior government source tells CTV News that Joly is meeting with Stellantis negotiator Pablo Di Si in Ottawa on Tuesday, and all four sides will meet again later this week.

In 2022, the federal government committed up to $529 million to Stellantis to retool both its plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont. Records show $222 million had been paid out as of March 2025.

With files from CTV News’ Marieke Walsh, CTV News’ Samantha Pope and CP24’s Bryann Aguilar

items.description: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem says falling global oil prices could mean inflation ends the year below the central bank’s last forecast.

items._ogDesc: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem says falling global oil prices could mean inflation ends the year below the central bank’s last forecast.
items.body:
Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem says falling global oil prices could mean inflation ends the year below the central bank’s last forecast.

The Bank of Canada said back in October that it saw inflation rising to 3.5 per cent by the end of the year as stubbornly high global oil prices threatened to put more pressure on consumers.

Statistics Canada said inflation held steady at 3.1 per cent in October. High gas prices from war in the Middle East continued to be the biggest driver of inflation, but the agency said upward pressure was broad-based across groceries and clothing as well.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Macklem suggested at a press conference in Toronto on Tuesday that recent relief at the gas pumps should mean inflation holds around those levels through the end of the year.

“The inflation forecast is a bit lower. Those costs that built up over the previous eight months, they’re still there, but there’s a bit of edge (that’s) come off the inflation forecast,” he said.

The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent October as it warned gas prices were staying higher for longer than first expected and inflationary pressures could start to spread.

Officials signalled at the time that they’d “proceed carefully,” but there could be a need for more rate hikes to come.

Macklem also addressed the current inflation outlook in a speech to the Economic Club of Canada in Toronto on Tuesday. While he acknowledged the recent climbdown in global benchmark oil prices, he said that wasn’t the only factor monetary policymakers were weighing.

“So far, businesses have largely absorbed the higher production and transport costs. But historical lags and our own business surveys suggest more pass-through to consumer prices in the year ahead. This second-round effect of the oil shock will add to inflation persistence,” he said in prepared remarks.

CIBC chief economist Avery Shenfeld said in a note to clients on Tuesday that the governor seemed to be downplaying the disinflationary impact of falling oil prices.

  • How to set BNN Bloomberg as your preferred source on Google

Shenfeld said Macklem’s focus on lingering inflation risks suggests the central bank could be gearing up to deliver a second consecutive rate hike at its next decision on Dec. 9.

“There was no direct reference to the December meeting, but what was apparent was that the governor was going out of his way to not show any changes in his thinking from October whenever possible,” he said.

Odds of a quarter-point hike from the Bank of Canada next month stood at 79 per cent as of Tuesday, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. That’s up from nearly 63 per cent on Monday.

Macklem said Tuesday the Bank of Canada will be weighing next week’s releases of gross domestic product data for the third quarter and November labour market figures before deciding what to do at its final policy rate decision of the year.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items.title: Drops for Nvidia, Anthropic and other AI stocks drag the U.S. market back down
items.description: AI stocks dragged the U.S. market lower after their surge from the day before quickly fizzled. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Traders work on the floor at the New York Stock Exchange in New York, Aug. 10, 2022. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig, file)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Seth Wenig</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: AI stocks dragged the U.S. market lower after their surge from the day before quickly fizzled. The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent.
items.body:
NEW YORK — Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence industry dragged the U.S. market lower Tuesday after their surge from the day before quickly fizzled. That’s even though much of the rest of Wall Street rose, along with confidence among Americans in the economy.

The S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent to its eighth loss in the last nine days. Tech stocks once again led the way and yanked the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 1.5 per cent. Stocks outside of AI held up much better, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 423 points, or 0.9 per cent.

They’re the latest swings for a market that’s been mostly sinking since hitting its all-time high last month. The worry is that prices for AI-related stocks shot too high into a possible bubble and need to deflate. That carries immense consequences for the broader market and workers’ 401(k) accounts because AI companies have grown into Wall Street’s most influential stocks.

While the surprise return of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO announced Monday does bring back a charismatic leader who championed the entire AI industry, it does not settle the deep concerns dogging it. For one, doubts remain about whether AI can possibly produce enough profit and productivity to make the massive investments underway in data centres worth it.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

At the same time, high interest rates make it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the industry’s growth. Sweeping victories for Democrats earlier this month in the U.S. midterm elections, meanwhile, have raised concerns about more regulation for AI, including possible halts to further construction of data centres.

To be sure, AI stocks and the broader U.S. market have been prone to extreme reversals since the summer, not only week to week but even hour to hour.

For now, at least, the momentum is back downward.

Nvidia fell 5.9 per cent a day after soaring 31.5 per cent to its biggest gain in more than two decades. Other stocks around the AI industry fell by similar amounts.

CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and rents out access to them over the cloud, tumbled 11.8 per cent. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, dropped 4.8 per cent.

And Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sank 6.5 per cent to drop below US$83. That’s how much Anthropic first sold its stock for in its initial public offering last week. The stock had briefly jumped as high as US$115 in its first day of trading amid a frenzy of hype.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

Such drops were powerful enough to drag the S&P 500 index lower even though most of the stocks within the index climbed. They rose following the latest report to say confidence among U.S. consumers is improving by more than economists expected.

Confidence jumped sharply for Democrats and independents following the midterm election results, according to the Conference Board. That narrowed the wide gap between them and Republicans, whose confidence fell slightly. The results echo a report from the University of Michigan released earlier in the month, which also showed a rise in overall sentiment following the midterm elections and a drop in oil prices from late October.

Companies in industries across the economy, meanwhile, continue to report strong growth in profits for the summer.

Dollar Tree climbed 11.2 per cent after reporting bigger earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. The average shopper spent slightly more in its stores during the three months than they did in last year’s third quarter, and more of them came in than last year.

Kohl’s rallied 19.5 per cent after reporting a profit for the latest quarter, when analysts were expecting basically zero. It also gave forecasts for revenue for the final three months of its fiscal year that were better than expected.

Businesses in the S&P 500 are on pace to report overall growth in earnings per share of more than 25 per cent for a third straight quarter, according to FactSet. That’s a big deal because stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits and interest rates over the long term. But emotions of investors can also overwhelm them in the short term, as the last few weeks have demonstrated.

All told, the S&P 500 fell 36.08 points to 7,201.09. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 423.39 to 50,018.70, and the Nasdaq composite fell 356.02 to 23,733.54.

  • Latest updates on investing here

In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.93 per cent from 4.92 per cent late Monday after drifting up and down earlier in the day.

Oil prices rose, which tend to push upward on inflation and on bond yields. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil climbed 2.4 per cent to US$88.78. It’s been yo-yoing between US$72 and US$114 since the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February.

In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed across Europe and Asia.

South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.3 per cent, and Japan’s Nikkei 225 rallied 3.9 per cent for two of the world’s bigger moves, as they caught up to Monday’s surge from Wall Street.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Writer Elaine Lai contributed to this report

items.title: Bank of Canada keeps 2% inflation target but adjusts what to track
items.description: The Bank of Canada is keeping firm to its two per cent inflation target, but it’s adjusting what it tracks to get there.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem waits to appear at the finance committee in Ottawa, Monday, May 4, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada is keeping firm to its two per cent inflation target, but it’s adjusting what it tracks to get there.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada is keeping firm to its two per cent inflation target, but it’s adjusting what it tracks to get there.

The federal government and the Bank of Canada renewed the central bank’s five-year mandate earlier this month and maintained the target for two per cent annual inflation, as measured by Statistics Canada’s consumer price index, or CPI.

The central bank maintains a one-to-three per cent band around that target, which offers some wiggle room to execute monetary policy.

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem spoke to a business crowd in Toronto on Tuesday where he hailed the two per cent target as a “clear and well-understood objective” since it was implemented in 1995.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Anchoring its policy rate decisions on that inflation target helped the Bank of Canada tame the post-COVID surge in inflation, Macklem argued in prepared remarks. But he acknowledged that Canadians didn’t respond well to inflation and the rate hikes it necessitated.

“For many Canadians, it was their first experience with high inflation. And they didn’t like it. As we reviewed our framework, we held consultations across the country to hear from Canadians. We heard a lot of anger,” Macklem said during a speech at the Economic Club of Canada on Tuesday.

The head of the Bank of Canada acknowledged the central bank could have done a better job in the post-pandemic period, which saw inflation pressures compound after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Monetary policymakers were “too slow to recognize the persistence of inflationary pressures and how broadly they were spreading through the economy,” Macklem said.

The Bank of Canada has updated its forecasting models to get a better handle on how supply shocks are likely to affect inflation and the economy, and whether monetary policy needs to intervene. Policymakers are also upping their communication efforts to get Canadians to go along with them on rate decisions.

Macklem acknowledged Tuesday that Bank of Canada has spurred confusion in the past over how it discussed underlying price trends.

The Bank of Canada previously downplayed its preferred measures of core inflation, CPI-trim and CPI-median, as it tried to gauge how supply shocks were affecting the economy.

“We wanted to be transparent about where we saw inflation pressures and where we did not. But we weren’t as clear as we hoped,” Macklem said.

“Canadians found it confusing when we discussed measures that strip out volatile prices such as food and gasoline. After all, these are important parts of the family budget. And financial market participants sometimes felt that we were moving the inflation goalposts.”

Excluding the right measures can help give the Bank of Canada a clearer picture of inflation trends and cut through temporary forces pushing prices higher, Macklem said.

Now, the Bank of Canada will put its focus back on an old measure called CPIX, which excludes eight fixed sets of items from the inflation calculation to provide a consistent benchmark of how prices are evolving.

The Bank of Canada used CPIX to guide monetary policy decisions from 2001 to 2016. Some of the items excluded from CPIX are gasoline, mortgage interest costs and fruits and vegetables.

Macklem helped develop CPIX as an indicator for the central bank 25 years ago. He told reporters after his speech Tuesday that the measure gives a more granular view of areas like food and energy by excluding the items most sensitive to temporary price fluctuations.

The Bank of Canada will retain what’s called CPI-trim as its other core measure, which strips out the items seeing the most extreme price changes in each month.

In tandem, the updated core inflation metrics give the Bank of Canada one view of a fixed basket of goods and services as well as one that adjusts based on what’s changing most rapidly.

“I think that gives you a diversity; hopefully the best of both worlds,” Macklem said.

The Bank of Canada will also start publishing an inflation dashboard on its website to show how various measures of price pressures are trending.

Macklem was asked in an armchair discussion after his speech what indicators economists should look at if they want to better gauge the Bank of Canada’s interest rate path — aside from headline inflation.

But the central bank governor laughed and brushed off the question.

“My pet peeve is that markets tend to focus — over-focus — on one or two indicators,” he said. “We have a big, complex economy that is highly connected to the world. You can’t summarize it in one or two indicators.”

Macklem explained that, while the Bank of Canada’s updated core metrics can help monetary policymakers see where prices are headed, keeping overall inflation at two per cent remains the central bank’s North Star.

“Total CPI inflation is our target, and it will be front and centre in all our communications. Various indicators help us understand where inflation is headed and the risks around that forecast. But they are inputs to our analysis, not targets,” he said.

In addition to shifting the core inflation metrics, the Bank of Canada’s new five-year mandate drops language from the previous statement about employment.

The 2021 mandate included an agreement with the federal government that monetary policy ought to support “maximum sustainable employment” when possible — a reference that’s absent from the 2026 renewal.

The new mandate also removed a previous allusion to the need to account for the impact of climate change on the Canadian economy and financial system.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: An Ontario Superior Court judge has dismissed a lawsuit that a raw chicken supplier had filed against Popeyes Louisiana Kitchen over the use of “unsafe” chicken.
items.body:
An Ontario Superior Court judge has dismissed a lawsuit that a raw chicken supplier had filed against Popeyes Louisiana Kitchen over the use of “unsafe” chicken.

The lawsuit was first filed by ADP Direct Poultry Ltd. on May 26, 2025. ADP alleged they lost their contract with the fried chicken chain after airing concerns over its “unsafe supply” of products.

But in a decision published on Nov. 19, Justice Lee Akazaki found ADP Direct Poultry Ltd.’s could not prove its “conspiracy theory” and said the accusation was “nothing short of a diversion from a deficient contract claim.”

“Instead of disclosing such additional facts of contract formation, ADP tries to overwhelm the court with a cinematic public-interest expose that Popeyes, a multinational restaurant chain, colluded with franchisees to lace the supply of its Ontario outlets with unsafe meat and to hide the practice from inspectors,” Justice Akazaki wrote.

“Even if ADP could back up its conspiracy theory with facts, its reward for blowing the whistle cannot be the court’s acceptance of an underdeveloped contract claim.”

  • How to set CP24 as your preferred source on Google
  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

ADP was an authorized chicken supplier for Popeyes in 2021 and 2022 but the court filings note that both parties allowed the contract to become null and void when it expired that February. ADP, however, kept filling orders until the end of 2024 and argued that the ongoing relationship “constituted a new supply agreement” that should have lasted until December, 2027.

In the lawsuit, ADP sought $35 million in contract damages from Popeyes, Restaurant Brands International (RBI) and Restaurant Services Canada Inc. (RSCI), plus $1 million in punitive damages. RBI is a Toronto-based company that owns Popeyes and RSCI is the supply chain manager.

Most of that $35 million was for lost profits through December 2027, according to the decision. The judge said continued orders don’t create a new contract and a projection of future orders is not a promise.

ADP also sued Popeyes, other meat suppliers and franchisees for $10.5 million from the alleged conspiracy to feed Ontario customers “unsafe chicken.” The supplier alleged raw chicken was stored in residential garages and transported in vehicles that did not have proper refrigeration to keep it from spoiling.

  • READ MORE: ‘Unsafe’: Popeyes accused of using supplier that stored chicken in residential garages

When the suit was filed, Popeyes said at the time that ADP was “lashing out after losing our business for a variety of legitimate reasons” and that it found “no evidence” to support the food safety allegations.

With regards to the alleged use of unsafe meat in the supply chain, Justice Akazaki said while the conspiracy could be the subject of a class action lawsuit by Popeyes customers who ingested it, it is not relevant to the contractual matter at hand.

Justice Akazaki also struck a defamation claim made by ADP over the “lashing out” comment. He noted how the lawsuit was filed after ADP lost Popeyes’ business and said a “reasonably informed person” reading the original statement of claim would see the fast-food chain’s response as defending itself against the “disproportionate reaction of a disgruntled trade supplier.”

The only part that of the lawsuit that survives is a breach of contract and misrepresentation claim against Popeyes Louisiana Kitchen and RBI, so long as ADP can file an amended claim within 30 days.

Justice Akazaki said these claims could still hold if ADP can show a supply agreement was in place after February 2023, that there was bad faith in the breach of agreement, and present material facts proving the deceit or fraud claim against Popeyes.

If ADP cannot do this, Popeyes can bring a motion for dismissal of the case, with costs.

items.description:

The single-month gain was the third-largest since COVID, and part of a much bigger wave of crisis-like borrowing not seen […]

The post Canada Is Borrowing Like It’s In Crisis, Killing Hopes For Mortgage Relief  appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Ottawa is borrowing at a crisis pace without a crisis—pushing federal bond debt to $1.33 trillion and keeping Canadian fixed mortgage rates stubbornly high.
items.body:
Canada may not be in crisis, but federal borrowing suggests it’s in the middle of a pandemic-like event. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows a historic surge in Government of Canada (GoC) direct bonds in October. The single-month gain was the third-largest since COVID, and part of a much bigger wave of crisis-like borrowing not seen outside of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) and the pandemic. This doesn’t just limit the country’s options to respond to the next crisis—it all but eliminates the possibility of fixed-rate mortgage relief.

Government of Canada Direct Bonds Just Hit $1.33 Trillion

Total balance of outstanding federal bond issuance.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Total direct bonds surged 1.7% (+$22.8B) to $1.33 trillion in October, up 9.8% (+$118.9B) from last year. After a tame September (+$280M), net issuance made the third-largest monthly jump in dollar terms outside of the 2020-2021 pandemic. It trails only April 2023 and July 2025.

The climb is part of a broader trend of persistently elevated growth. Ottawa’s borrowing has logged 26 straight months of annual growth above 6% after the October gain. Over the past three years, the total has increased a mind-boggling 29.2% (+$301.7B). That’s right. Nearly 1 in 4 dollars of federal bond debt was added within three years, outside of the pandemic.

Canada’s Crisis-Like Borrowing Without A Crisis

Canadian policymakers are borrowing at a crisis pace without a crisis. Over the past 12 months, nominal dollar growth was 40.2% larger than the peak 12-month surge during the GFC. Outside of the GFC (2009-2012) and COVID (2020-2022), the balance hasn’t run this close to 10% annual growth since 1997. That was the tail end of Canada’s 1990s fiscal crunch, just as the last major real estate downturn was bottoming out.

The scale of borrowing won’t be easy to shake off. Since February 2020, the net bond balance has climbed 114.8%, more than doubling from pre-pandemic levels. Following a brief dip in 2023, growth came back with a vengeance—averaging 9.4% y/y over the past 24 months. That’s well above the 2010-2019 average of 6.6% on a much larger base. This has created a structural problem.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer has warned that interest payments will consume almost 1 in 7 dollars of revenue by 2030-31. More borrowing has driven debt-servicing costs to grow 29.5% faster than revenue, according to the agency. That would require nearly impossible revenue growth to catch up.

Ottawa’s Bond Supply Is Bad News For Mortgage Rate Relief

Heavy bond supply is set to put a drag on mortgage borrowing. Unlike variable mortgages that track the Bank of Canada’s overnight policy rate, fixed-rate loans are based on GoC bond yields (primarily the 5-year). The medium- and long-term impact of the bond balance may be abstract and debatable, but the short-term impact is crystal clear. It will limit any downside for mortgage rates, helping to build a floor.

For context, the GoC 5-year bond yield sat at 3.4% this morning, 74 basis points higher than last year. Those hoping for good news ahead of their mortgage renewal may not be so lucky, with BMO telling investors that rate relief is done for this phase of the cycle.

items.title: Mortgage delinquency rate up 31% in Q3, driven by Ontario and B.C.: Equifax report
items.description: TORONTO — A new report suggests there's growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.
items._ogDesc: TORONTO — A new report suggests there's growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.
items.body:
TORONTO — A new report suggests there's growing stress among homeowners, with some struggling to keep up with monthly mortgage payments as interest rates rise again.

Equifax Canada's third-quarter consumer credit trends report says the national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate — defined as missed payments three months in a row — reached 0.32 per cent, the highest since the credit agency started tracking the metric in 2013.

That's up 31.1 per cent year-over-year, mainly pushed higher by missed mortgage payments in Ontario and British Columbia.

"That's the highest we've seen, particularly for Ontario. And it's still going up," said Rebecca Oakes, Equifax Canada's vice-president of advanced analytics, said in an interview.

"That's the biggest concern for us."

The Equifax data echoes the findings of a recent a TD report, which showed Ontario's mortgage arrears have nearly tripled from pre-pandemic levels to approach their 2008 financial crisis peak.

"This reflects elevated mortgage balances and greater sensitivity to borrowing costs," wrote TD economist Maria Solovieva in the report published last week.

Growing pressure on households comes as the Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 2.5 per cent last month for the first time in more than three years, amid concerns that higher energy prices could spill into broader inflation.

The move prompted the big banks to raise their prime rates, which is used to set interest rates on a range of loans including variable-rate mortgages.

Equifax estimates about 1.4 million Canadians have a variable-rate mortgage out of a total 9.1 million homeowners. Another 1.3 million consumers also have a home equity line of credit, or HELOC, balance of more than $50,000.

Every quarter-point rate hike adds roughly $860 million a year in interest on variable-rate mortgages, the company estimates.

Oakes suspects mortgage delinquencies will continue to rise in the coming months, depending on changes to interest rates.

"If interest rates stay relatively flat from this point on, I'd expect to see it ease off in the middle of next year," she said.

But if more hikes come in, "it's just going to put additional pressure."

The central bank is expected to make its last rate decision of the year on Dec. 9.

Financial market odds for a quarter-point rate hike was 63 per cent as of Monday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics.

Oakes said first-time homebuyers and younger Canadians may bear the brunt of rising rates because they tend to carry a higher-balance mortgage.

Still, she said mortgage delinquencies overall are less than one per cent.

"It's quite small, you know, from that standpoint, but of course it knocks on to other types of credit, like credit cards, auto loans," Oakes said.

"That's where those individuals miss the payments first rather than on the mortgage itself."

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem said Tuesday that he doesn't see rising mortgage delinquencies as a threat to the economy.

"Obviously for some people, this is very tough," he said in Toronto at an unrelated press conference. "But for the economy as a whole, it's not a huge headwind."Credit card balances reached $136.2 billion in the third quarter, up 4.82 per cent from a year earlier, the Equifax data showed.

Overall, total Canadian consumer debt was $2.74 trillion in the third quarter, up 4.68 per cent from a year ago.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 24, 2026.

Ritika Dubey, The Canadian Press

items.description: Variable-rate borrowers and condo owners face the sharpest exposure as delinquencies keep climbing
items.content: <p>Variable-rate borrowers and condo owners face the sharpest exposure as delinquencies keep climbing</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639311422146198704.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Variable-rate borrowers and condo owners face the sharpest exposure as delinquencies keep climbing
items.body:
The Bank of Canada's first rate increase since 2023 arrives at precisely the wrong moment for a broad cohort of Canadian homeowners.

Delinquency rates have been climbing without interruption for four years, borrowers who bought near the 2022 peak are sitting on negative equity, and those with variable-rate mortgages are about to feel the latest quarter-point move almost immediately.

New data from Equifax Canada puts the full picture in one number: the national 90-plus day mortgage delinquency rate has reached its highest level since tracking began 13 years ago.

Missed payments across three or more consecutive months climbed to 0.32%, up 31.1% year over year. It marks the sixteenth consecutive quarterly increase.

Ontario and British Columbia accounted for 91% of annual growth in severely delinquent mortgage accounts, while total Canadian consumer debt reached $2.74 trillion in Q3 2026, up 4.68% from the same period a year earlier.

Variable-rate borrowers bear the first blow

Of Canada's 9.1 million mortgage holders, approximately 1.4 million carry variable-rate mortgages.

A further 1.3 million consumers hold a home equity line of credit (HELOC) balance above $50,000.

Every quarter-point rate increase adds roughly $860 million annually in interest costs on variable-rate mortgages and approximately $419 million on HELOCs, according to Equifax Canada.

"A rate increase does not have the same impact on every homeowner on the same day," said Rebecca Oakes, Vice President of Advanced Analytics at Equifax Canada, in Ontario.

"Variable-rate borrowers can feel the impact of a rate increase within weeks, while others may not experience the effect until they renew or refinance. With the Bank of Canada's next interest rate decision scheduled for December 9, the group to watch are those homeowners with the least room to absorb another increase."

Brokers are fielding that pressure firsthand. Joel Fox, chief operating officer of Ownright in Canada, explained in an interview with Canadian Mortgage Professional how compounding renewal costs are bearing down on already-stretched mortgage holders.

"Plenty of people locked in at very low rates a few years ago, and they're now renewing into a much bigger payment. This hike doesn't help," he said.

His advice to clients approaching renewal: "If you're renewing in the next year, start early. Talk to your lender or broker, compare offers and know what your payment will be before the renewal notice shows up."

New Ratehub .ca data shows home affordability declined across all 13 major Canadian housing markets in October as rising mortgage rates increased income requirements for buyers. https://t.co/2l9ocHRMfL — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 19, 2026

Negative equity rising among Ontario condo owners

The dollar value of severely delinquent mortgages is growing faster than the actual count of delinquent accounts — a signal, Oakes noted, that larger-balance borrowers are increasingly under strain. 

Negative equity — where the amount owed on a property exceeds its current market value — has become concentrated in specific segments.

Ontario accounts for an estimated 70% of Canadian mortgages currently in negative equity, representing 5% of all provincial mortgages, compared with 1.85% in British Columbia.

Among condo owners, the exposure rises to 7.2%, against 2.7% for freehold properties. For buyers who entered the market in 2022 near the peak, negative equity risk reaches 8.4%.

"Negative equity is still relatively uncommon in Canada, but what stands out is how concentrated it has become," Oakes said.

"For most of these homeowners it isn't an immediate problem as long as they can keep up with their payments. The challenge comes if they need to sell or refinance."

Victor Tran, mortgage and real estate expert at Rates.ca in Canada, described a gradual but sustained upward path for mortgage delinquencies in Canada during a February interview with CMP. 

"I think [delinquencies] will continue to increase as more homeowners renew their mortgages in the next 12 months, 24 months even. But I think it's going to be a slow grind," he said.

items.title: Canadian mortgage market rewards adaptable brokers in 2026
items.description: Max Singh of TMG The Mortgage Group sees opportunity in a year defined by strategic client decisions
items.content: <p>Max Singh of TMG The Mortgage Group sees opportunity in a year defined by strategic client decisions</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0311_638367747040950607.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Max Singh of TMG The Mortgage Group sees opportunity in a year defined by strategic client decisions
items.body:
The Canadian mortgage market is not short of challenges in 2026, but for Calgary-based broker Max Singh of TMG The Mortgage Group (pictured top), difficulty and opportunity are two sides of the same coin.

Singh describes a Canadian mortgage market shaped by affordability pressures, bond market volatility, and a record renewal wave, with the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) projecting 1.15 million mortgage renewals in 2026, the largest concentration in recent history.

"I would describe 2026 as a year of adjustment and opportunity," Singh told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

"Compared to last year, I've noticed clients becoming much more strategic about their mortgage decisions, whether that's purchasing, refinancing or renewing."

Navigating a shifting lending landscape

Tightening lender guidelines and heightened scrutiny around income verification and debt servicing have defined the operational challenge of 2026 for Singh.

"With bond market volatility, changing lender guidelines and increased scrutiny around income and debt servicing, mortgage brokers need to be more knowledgeable and adaptable than ever," he said.

"I've always believed our greatest value comes from understanding the client's complete financial picture and having the experience and relationships to find solutions when traditional lending doesn't quite fit."

His assessment aligns with CMP's latest market analysis of the risks facing Canadian mortgage brokers.

Lindsay Zwart, Equifax Canada's director of solutions for mortgage and housing, reinforced the point at MortgageFest Canada in Toronto in September.

"Risking a borrower in 2026 does not look the same as risking a borrower in 2016, in 2019, and in 2020," Zwart told delegates.

"As a broker, your two most valuable currencies are your time and your reputation in the industry with your lenders."

Mortgage Professionals Canada's 2026 consumer survey, cited in CMP's 2026 Brokers on Lenders special report, puts broker market share at 38% in 2025, a six-percentage-point annual gain and the highest level on record.

Looking ahead to 2027

Singh expects confidence to build gradually rather than through dramatic rate reductions.

"I'm cautiously optimistic about 2027," he said.

"I believe we'll see opportunities as economic conditions evolve, buyers regain confidence and homeowners continue reviewing their mortgage options. I don't necessarily anticipate dramatic interest rate reductions, but I do expect clients to become increasingly comfortable making financial decisions rather than waiting indefinitely for the perfect market."

CMP's annual ranking of Canada's 75 best mortgage brokers — professionals who collectively moved more than $10 billion — illustrates the relational model Singh champions.

"Whether it's reaching out six to nine months before renewal, conducting annual mortgage reviews or simply checking in, I believe the brokers who invest in relationships, education and proactive mortgage management will be the ones who really thrive in 2027."

The motivation goes deeper than deal volume.

"At the end of the day, we're not just arranging mortgages; we're helping people build wealth, achieve homeownership and make better financial decisions for their families. That's what keeps me passionate about this business," Singh said.

items.title: Ontario mortgage arrears near crisis peak as rates take toll
items.description: A TD Economics report shows Ontario's arrears rate has nearly tripled since the pandemic
items.content: <p>A TD Economics report shows Ontario's arrears rate has nearly tripled since the pandemic</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639311370259041851.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A TD Economics report shows Ontario's arrears rate has nearly tripled since the pandemic
items.body:
Canadian consumers are expected to "bend, but not break" – but nowhere is that strain more visible than in Ontario, where mortgage arrears have nearly tripled from pre-pandemic norms.

A November report by TD Economics economist Maria Solovieva, CFA, finds the province's arrears rate hit 0.34% in August, approaching the 0.43% peak of the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) from a pre-pandemic baseline of just 0.12%.

While national real consumer spending grew at a nearly 3% pace through the first half of 2026, Solovieva cautions that "solid spending growth masks pockets of financial strain, particularly in Ontario."

Consumer insolvency rates, though still below GFC-era highs, have trended upward since the rate-hiking cycle began in 2022, and the most recent reading "suggests a renewed upward pressure, warranting close monitoring," the report states.

TransUnion's financial stress indicator, also tracked by the Bank of Canada, reached a new high of 2.23% in Q2 2026, roughly 25 basis points above its pre-pandemic average. 

New Ratehub .ca data shows home affordability declined across all 13 major Canadian housing markets in October as rising mortgage rates increased income requirements for buyers. https://t.co/2l9ocHRMfL — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) November 19, 2026

What rising arrears mean for brokers and their clients

Ontario's vulnerability traces to the pandemic housing boom. As CMP's analysis of Ontario and BC delinquency trends confirmed, buyers near the 2021–22 price peak carry larger balances and thinner equity, while BC 's rate of increase has started to slow.

The TD Economics report notes that "even at today's elevated rate, roughly one in 300 Ontario mortgages is in arrears," and that "the greatest vulnerability likely lies among those who purchased near the 2021–22 housing market peak, when prices were highest and equity cushions may be thinnest."

Leah Zlatkin, licensed mortgage broker and LowestRates.ca expert, told Canadian Mortgage Professional in May that the data demands vigilance: "Mortgage delinquency is often one of the last signs of financial strain, because most homeowners will cut back in other areas before missing a mortgage payment," Zlatkin said.

"That's why even a small increase in arrears is worth paying attention to. It can suggest that some households have already used savings, leaned on credit, or reduced everyday spending to keep up. For borrowers coming up for renewal, the question isn't only whether they can make the next payment, but whether payments can be sustained over time."

Statistics Canada data cited in the TD Economics report show more than 35% of households in Oshawa, Windsor, and Hamilton, Ontario are struggling to meet their financial needs – the highest rates among Canada's largest cities – with all three cities reporting unemployment above the national average.

Labour market is the bigger swing factor

The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by 25 basis points in October, with another increase expected in January 2027.

Variable-rate mortgages account for a historically high 35% of outstanding mortgages in Canada.

The report estimates roughly $115 in additional annual mortgage servicing costs relative to earlier forecasts; in Ontario, the figure rises to approximately $140 annually – on top of a servicing burden already around $2,250 above the national average.

Those increases are "unlikely to be the straw that breaks the camel's back, but they represent another expense for households whose budgets are already stretched by higher inflation," Solovieva writes.

Victor Tran, mortgage and real estate expert at Rates.ca, told CMP earlier this year that a dramatic escalation remained unlikely: "I think [delinquencies] will continue to increase as more homeowners renew their mortgages in the next 12 months, 24 months even. But I think it's going to be a slow grind," he said.

"It's not going to be a significant, drastic increase suddenly and I don't think we're going to see sudden mass foreclosures or power of sales. At the end of the day, the banks and lenders out there are in business to help homeowners out and lend them money, not to foreclose on homes."

TD Economics forecasts Ontario's arrears to plateau near mid-2027, declining in the second half of the year as employment conditions improve.

The principal risk is clear: "if weak hiring gives way to widespread job losses, pushing the unemployment rate higher, mortgage arrears could rise further and remain elevated for longer."

For now, the report's conclusion stands – "households in Ontario and across Canada are expected to bend, but not break."

items._ogDesc: Executive tells CMP why the lending giant is backing the prestigious industry awards
items.body:
MCAN Financial Group is backing the 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) as sponsor for one of its most important honours, the MCAN Award for Woman of Distinction, with the 20th edition of the ceremony set to take place on Wednesday (November 25) at Rebel Toronto.

The awards are an important opportunity to celebrate the people behind an industry that’s as essential as ever to helping Canadians achieve their homebuying dreams, according to MCAN’s director of corporate brand and marketing Kim Mercer.

“MCAN is proud to support the Canadian Mortgage Awards because at its core this industry is about people,” she told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “The CMAs give us a chance to set competition aside and celebrate what we’re all working toward: helping Canadians make it home.”

With mortgage professionals set to congregate in Toronto from across the whole country for the star-studded ceremony, Mercer said the evening was also about connection.

“It’s an opportunity to recognize the brokers, teams and partners who show up for their clients and communities every day, and the people and partnerships that keep our industry moving forward,” she said.

“It’s also a fun night to reconnect with colleagues, celebrate success, and cheer on the award nominees.”

Mercer said the MCAN team is especially excited about the nomination of Cam Dellipizzi, one of 10 shortlisted for Lender BDM of the Year (Prime).

The value of relationships

The case for celebrating excellence comes back to relationships, Mercer said, at a time when the connection between brokers and lenders has arguably never been more important.

“This is a relationship-driven business, and excellence often comes down to how many people show up for their clients and partners, especially when the market is complex,” she said.

The event takes place at a significant moment for the mortgage and housing markets, with affordability challenges and rising interest rates continuing to present hurdles for Canadian homebuyers and owners.

That’s part of the reason mortgage professionals are such a valuable component of the housing sector, Mercer suggested. “After a year of uncertainty, it’s important to celebrate what makes this industry such a powerful part of Canadians’ homeownership journeys: the people,” she said.

“Recognizing great work gives us a chance to celebrate the people raising the bar and reminds all of us what great service and partnership can look like.”

MCAN’s 2026 and 2027 focuses

With 2027 just around the corner, the industry is reflecting on the year that’s been and looking ahead to what’s in store for the coming 12 months.

Mercer paid tribute to the brokers working with MCAN to help Canadians navigate the current market, and highlighted opportunities in store next year. “We’re incredibly grateful for the support of our broker partners and the trust they place in us to deliver for their clients,” she said.

“This year challenged all of us to be more flexible and thoughtful about how we help Canadians navigate homeownership. For MCAN, that means continuing to listen and invest in our people, products, technology and experience, making it easier for brokers to find responsible solutions for real-life client needs.”

On the product side, Mercer said MCAN had worked to keep its mortgage solutions in step with what’s most important to brokers in a constantly evolving market. “A big focus for us has been making sure our mortgage solutions keep pace with what brokers are actually seeing across Canada,” she said.

And the lender has also invested in how brokers work with it. “We’ve continued investing in the overall partner experience through our regional teams, technology, clearer pricing and programs like SCORE and ICON that create value beyond the transaction,” she said.

Meanwhile, the company has kept its partner events going in 2026, with Summits and Connects continuing in Vancouver, Ottawa, Calgary and Spain. Next year’s destination is Porto. “Great partnerships should deliver great business and a little fun along the way,” Mercer said.

As the industry prepares to celebrate its top performers at the CMAs – and toast the importance of strong connections and partnerships – Mercer said the human side of the business remains paramount.

“One thing that continues to stand out to us is that every mortgage file represents a person, a family and a story,” she said. “We believe the good stuff happens when brokers and lenders understand that full picture and work together to find a responsible path forward. That’s the kind of partnership we want to keep building in 2027.”

items.title: Finmo's Sidekick: the AI assistant that knows your deals
items.description: Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call
items.content: <p>Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0321_639307939243156766.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Lendesk's new release takes AI from single tasks to whole deals, and the broker always makes the call
items.body:
Most brokers have tried AI tools to draft emails and answer quick questions. What they haven't had is an AI assistant that knows their deals and can work on them.

Lendesk built Sidekick to close that gap. Sidekick launched in open beta at Finmo Momentum 2026 on November 24 and it's a new AI assistant inside Finmo, Lendesk's mortgage origination platform. It runs in a chat panel next to the broker's deals, where it reads the application and documents, makes updates on request, and looks up lender rates and guidelines. The broker never has to leave the deal.

“We wanted to give brokers a tool that actually works the deal, instead of just surfacing information about it. Sidekick knows the deal, knows the lenders, and takes on the admin, so brokers can spend more time with clients,” said Carter Zimmerman, president of Lendesk.

From single tasks to the whole deal

Each of Finmo's earlier AI tools did one job. In 2024, Finmo added AI deal create, which builds a new application from an email chain, call transcript or notes, and AI fill from document, which pulls property details from an MLS listing into the deal. This year Finmo added AI down payment verification and income verification, which cut hours of document review down to minutes.

Sidekick works differently. It doesn't run one fixed process. It can help with any task a broker does in Finmo: building and editing deals, managing documents, running down payment and income verification, calculating GDS/TDS, and researching lenders.

“Our first AI tools each solved one problem well. Sidekick ties them together,” Zimmerman said. “For the first time, a broker can ask for help the way they’d ask a colleague and get it across the whole deal.”

Ask Sidekick to organize and review a deal’s documents, and it renames files consistently, moves them into the right document conditions, and adds any missing conditions. It then runs down payment and income verification.

Ask Sidekick which rental income approach works best for a conventional deal, and it compares lenders’ add-back and offset policies using Lender Spotlight. It estimates the impact on GDS/TDS and compares available rates and requirements, helping identify the best fit and the lowest-rate option that meets the lender’s stated qualifying limits.

“Sidekick takes what you thought was a B deal and turns it into an A deal,” said Joe Tomkins, Director of User Development & Enablement at Lendesk.

Placing the deal

Sidekick connects to Lender Spotlight, so it can match a deal against lender policies and pull current rates. The "Place this deal" flow works the deal the way an experienced broker would. It grades the deal, screens lenders on their guidelines, and compares rates. Then it gives one recommendation, with a short list of alternatives.

“Finding the right lender for a deal takes experience, plus a lot of checking rates and guidelines across dozens of lenders,” Zimmerman said. “Sidekick handles the checking in one request, so brokers get to the right shortlist faster.”

The broker makes the call

By default, Sidekick asks before it changes anything. Each update, whether it's an edit to the application or a credit pull, shows up as an approval card with the exact change. Nothing is saved until the broker approves it. Read-only tasks, like reviewing the deal or running GDS/TDS numbers, happen right away.

Sidekick also works within the broker's own permissions, so it can only see and do what that broker already can in Finmo — and brokers can delete their chat history at any time.

“In mortgages, trust isn't optional,” Zimmerman said. “That's why Sidekick shows every change before it's made. The broker is always in control.”

Sidekick is available now in open beta, free while the beta runs. Brokers already on Finmo can ask their team admin to turn it on through Finmo support. Brokers new to Finmo can sign up and request access when they join.

items._ogDesc: Canadian household debt hit $3.3T in September as mortgage growth fell to a 25-year low, while consumer credit ran hot on rising distress borrowing.
items.body:
Canadian household debt is slowing in growth, but it doesn’t appear to be voluntary deleveraging. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows household credit climbed in September, though mortgages are contributing less. The segment grew at one of the slowest paces in a quarter-century, even as consumer credit took off alongside rising distress borrowing.

Canadian Household Debt Hits $3.3 Trillion Even As Growth Slows

Annual growth of Canadian household credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Canadian household debt climbed 0.3% (+$9.4 billion) to hit $3.3 trillion in September, 3.7% (+$119.3 billion) higher than last year. It’s a sharp deceleration from the 4.6% annual growth reported this time a year ago, suggesting household borrowing is slowing. Even at a slower pace, adding over $119 billion in a single year is hardly deleveraging. Households are just lightly tapping the brakes.

Canadian Mortgage Credit Growth Slows To Lowest Pace In 25 Years

Annual growth of Canadian mortgage credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Mortgage growth appears to be the big drag here. Outstanding mortgage credit rose 0.2% (+$4.9 billion) to $2.47 trillion in September, 3.5% (+$82.6 billion) from last year. This is the slowest annual growth for mortgage credit since mid-2001. In an economy as housing-dependent as Canada’s, a quarter-century low in mortgage expansion signals that buyers are either tapped out or stuck on the sidelines.

Distress Borrowing Keeps Consumer Credit Running Hot At $847 Billion

Annual growth of Canadian non-mortgage household credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

One area of credit growth that continues to run hot is consumer credit. Households grew non-mortgage debt by 0.5% (+$4.5 billion) to $847.0 billion in September, up 4.5% (+$36.7 billion). While slower than August, the annual growth of this segment has been higher than usual over the past few years, sustaining levels the country hasn’t seen since mid-2010. Healthy credit growth can sometimes be a sign of strong consumers, but this isn’t one of those times.

Credit reporting bureaus are increasingly attributing growth to distress borrowing. Firms like TransUnion have noted that more borrowers are carrying higher balances as they use credit to make ends meet. Mortgage borrowers aren’t much better, with the bureau also explaining that a rising share of mortgage debt is due to accumulating balances, not originations.

Slowing headline growth may look like restraint on the surface, but it’s a more ominous sign. There are few signs of relief ahead, as the market expects higher borrowing costs.

items.title: M3’s Bernard talks CMAs, importance of recognizing top performers
items.description: Broker network backs the Canadian Mortgage Awards as brokers gain ground in a tough market
items.content: <p>Broker network backs the Canadian Mortgage Awards as brokers gain ground in a tough market</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639275163379725593.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Broker network backs the Canadian Mortgage Awards as brokers gain ground in a tough market
items.body:
The Canadian Mortgage Awards (CMAs) finally arrive this week – and as the event’s social media sponsor, M3 Financial Group is backing the brokers, lenders, and service providers shortlisted across multiple categories.

The event, set to take place at Rebel Toronto on November 25, will celebrate its 20th anniversary this year. Luc Bernard, chairman and chief executive officer of M3, told Canadian Mortgage Professional that paying tribute to the industry’s best performers was an essential part of ensuring the sector goes from strength to strength.

“We feel that it is of utmost importance to celebrate the mortgage broker industry and recognize the top performers,” he said. Being in a room with the sector’s highest achievers, he said, “obliges us to continue elevating our work year after year.”

The event draws nominations from brokers, brokerages, lenders, underwriters, business development managers (BDMs), and industry service providers across the country. Nominations closed in August, with the shortlisted Excellence Awardees published last month.

Brokers can be recognized regionally, with separate awards for Eastern Canada (Quebec and Ontario), the Maritimes and Atlantic Canada, and Western Canada, or by specialty – with awards for alternative, private lending, reverse mortgage and commercial brokers.

Brokerages and teams compete by size, alongside awards for national broker networks, national brokerages and new brokerages. On the lending side, BDMs and underwriters are recognized in both prime and specialist (alternative and private) categories. Industry service providers, innovators and employers of choice round out the field.

All you need to know about the award categories

Several awards put the spotlight on people. Twelve brokers are shortlisted for Young Achiever of the Year, 11 for The MCAN Award for Woman of Distinction, and nine for The REMIC Award for Finfluencer of the Year, (see CMP's full list of 2026 Canadian Mortgage Awards excellence awardees here).

The fields vary in size. The regional broker awards each have 10 or 11 shortlisted brokers, while the private lending and commercial categories have seven each, the reverse mortgage category three, and the National Broker Network of the Year category four.

Sponsors have also put their names on individual awards, including The EQ Bank Award for Broker of the Year – Reverse Mortgages and The Grechi Carter Professional Corporation Award for Broker of the Year – Commercial. The Haventree Bank Award for Lifetime Achievement, the programme's highest honour, has no shortlist and will be announced only on the night.

Brokers shine in challenging times

The industry’s top performers have shone in a challenging market this year, one that’s brought the importance of mortgage brokers into even sharper focus.

The ongoing trade war with the US, and price pressures caused by the US-Iran conflict, have weighed against the housing market outlook for 2026 as affordability challenges and rising interest rates also leave their mark.

But brokers are coming to the fore in turbulent times that have also seen a wave of mortgage renewals in 2025 and 2026 at much higher rates than the original contract.

Overall broker market share reached 38% last year, according to Mortgage Professionals Canada’s (MPC’s) most recent consumer survey – a jump of six percentage points from the year before.

Nearly two in five Canadians took out their most recent mortgage through a broker in 2025, a new high for the channel, with the share climbing to 48% among recent first-time buyers.

For M3, a key focus of the year has been broker education, with the aim of equipping brokers to be “the best that they can be for future Canadian homeowners.”

Bernard said the night is also a reminder of the bigger goal. “Let’s all work together to grow this industry, allowing more Canadians to trust brokers with the biggest purchase of their lives,” he said.
